title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: It was past one in the morning when Pierre left his friend's house. It was a cloudless northern summer night. Pierre hailed an open cab, intending to drive straight home. But the closer he got to his house, the more impossible it seemed to go to sleep on a night like this. It was bright enough to see far down the empty street, and it felt more like dawn or dusk than the middle of the night. On the way, Pierre remembered that Anatole Kuragin was expecting the usual crowd for cards that evening, after which there would typically be a drinking session, ending with the kind of amusements Pierre was particularly fond of.
"I should go to Kuragin's," he thought.

But he immediately remembered his promise to Prince Andrew not to go. Then, as happens with people of weak character, he wanted so desperately to enjoy those familiar pleasures one more time that he decided to go anyway. The thought immediately came to him that his promise to Prince Andrew didn't really count, because he had already promised Prince Anatole he would come before he gave Andrew his word. "Besides," he told himself, "all these 'words of honor' are just social conventions with no real meaning — especially when you consider that you could be dead by tomorrow, or something so extraordinary might happen that honor and dishonor become equally meaningless!" Pierre often talked himself out of his own decisions with reasoning like this. He went to Kuragin's.

When he reached the large house near the Horse Guards barracks where Anatole lived, Pierre walked through the lit entrance, climbed the stairs, and went in through the open door. There was no one in the front hall; empty bottles, cloaks, and boots were scattered around; there was a smell of alcohol, and from somewhere deeper in the house came shouting and the sound of voices.

Cards and supper were over, but the guests had not yet left. Pierre tossed off his cloak and entered the first room, where the remains of supper lay on the table. A footman, thinking no one was watching, was secretly finishing off what was left in the glasses. From a third room came bursts of laughter, the shouting of familiar voices, the growling of a bear, and general chaos. About eight or nine young men were crowded anxiously around an open window. Three others were roughhousing with a young bear — one pulling it by its chain, trying to set it on the others.
"A hundred on Stevens!" shouted one.
"No holding on!" cried another.
"I'm betting on Dolokhov!" yelled a third. "Kuragin, separate their hands!"
"Leave the bear alone — there's a bet to settle!"
"One go — or he loses!" shouted a fourth.

"Jacob, bring a bottle!" shouted the host — a tall, handsome young man standing in the middle of the group, coatless, his fine linen shirt unbuttoned at the chest. "Hold on, boys — here's Petya! Good man!" he called out, turning to Pierre.

From the window, another voice rang out — a man of medium height with clear blue eyes, his tone strikingly sober among all the drunken shouting: "Come here — settle the bets!" This was Dolokhov, an officer of the Semenov regiment, a notorious gambler and duelist who was living with Anatole. Pierre smiled and looked around cheerfully.
"I don't understand. What's going on?"
"Wait — he hasn't had enough to drink yet! A bottle here," said Anatole, and snatching a glass from the table, he went over to Pierre.
"First things first — you have to drink!"

Pierre drained one glass after another, peering from under his brows at the rowdy guests who had crowded back around the window, and listening to their chatter. Anatole kept refilling Pierre's glass while explaining that Dolokhov had made a bet with Stevens, an English naval officer, that he could drink an entire bottle of rum while sitting on the outer ledge of the third-floor window with his legs dangling over the edge.
"Come on, drink it all," said Anatole, handing Pierre the last glass, "or I won't let you go!"
"No, that's enough," said Pierre, pushing Anatole aside, and he walked up to the window.
Dolokhov was gripping the Englishman's hand and repeating the terms of the bet clearly and precisely, addressing himself mainly to Anatole and Pierre.

Dolokhov was of medium height, with curly hair and light blue eyes. He was about twenty-five. Like all infantry officers, he wore no mustache, so his mouth — the most striking feature of his face — was clearly visible. The lines of that mouth were remarkably well defined. The middle of his upper lip formed a sharp point and pressed firmly against the lower one, and something like two separate smiles played constantly around the corners; combined with the bold, insolent intelligence in his eyes, this created a face impossible to overlook. Dolokhov was a man without money or connections. Yet despite the fact that Anatole spent tens of thousands of rubles, Dolokhov lived with him and had established himself so firmly that everyone who knew them — including Anatole himself — respected Dolokhov more than they respected Anatole. He could play any card game and nearly always won. No matter how much he drank, he never lost his composure. Both Kuragin and Dolokhov were at that time notorious among the wild set of Petersburg.

The bottle of rum was brought. Two footmen, clearly rattled by the shouting and orders of the young gentlemen, were working to force out the window frame that prevented anyone from sitting on the outer sill.
Anatole strutted up to the window with his usual swagger. He wanted to smash something. Shoving the footmen aside, he grabbed the frame and tugged, but couldn't budge it. He smashed a pane of glass.
"You have a go, Hercules," he said, turning to Pierre.
Pierre grabbed the crossbeam, pulled hard, and ripped the oak frame out with a crash.
"Take it all the way out, or they'll think I'm holding on," said Dolokhov.
"Is the Englishman backing out? Hm? Are we ready?" said Anatole.
"All set," said Pierre, watching Dolokhov approach the window with the bottle of rum in his hand. Through the opening, the light of the sky was visible — dawn blending into the last glow of sunset.
Dolokhov jumped onto the windowsill, the bottle still in his hand. "Listen!" he called out, standing there and addressing the room. Everyone fell silent.

"I bet fifty imperials" — he spoke in French so the Englishman could understand, though his French wasn't very good — "I bet fifty imperials... or would you prefer to make it a hundred?" he added, turning to the Englishman.
"No, fifty," the Englishman replied.

"Fine. Fifty imperials that I will drink an entire bottle of rum without taking it from my mouth, sitting out there on that ledge" — he leaned down and pointed to the sloping surface outside the window — "with my legs hanging over the edge and without holding on to anything. Agreed?"
"Agreed," said the Englishman.
Anatole turned to the Englishman and, grasping one of his coat buttons and looking down at him — the Englishman was short — began repeating the terms of the wager in English.

"Wait!" Dolokhov shouted, banging the bottle on the windowsill to get everyone's attention. "Hold on, Kuragin. Listen! If anyone else does the same thing, I'll pay him a hundred imperials. Understood?"

The Englishman nodded but gave no sign of whether he intended to take up this challenge himself. Anatole wouldn't let go of him, and although the Englishman kept nodding to show he understood, Anatole went on translating Dolokhov's words into English. A thin young fellow — a hussar of the Life Guards who had been losing all evening — climbed onto the windowsill, leaned out, and looked down.
"Oh! Oh! Oh!" he murmured, staring down at the stone pavement.
"Get back!" Dolokhov shouted, shoving him away from the window. The young man stumbled awkwardly back into the room, tripping over his spurs.

Setting the bottle on the windowsill within easy reach, Dolokhov climbed slowly and carefully through the window and lowered his legs. He braced himself against both sides of the frame, settled into position, shifted a little to the right, then to the left, and picked up the bottle. Anatole brought two candles and set them on the sill, though it was already quite light. Dolokhov's back in its white shirt and his curly head were lit from both sides. Everyone crowded to the window — the Englishman in front. Pierre stood there smiling, saying nothing. One man, older than the rest, suddenly pushed forward with a look of alarm and anger and tried to grab Dolokhov's shirt.
"This is madness! He'll be killed!" said this more sensible man.
Anatole stopped him.
"Don't touch him! You'll startle him, and then he really will fall. Eh? What then? Eh?"
Dolokhov turned around and, gripping with both hands again, readjusted himself on his perch.
"If anyone interferes again," he said, squeezing the words out through his thin, compressed lips, "I'll throw him down there myself. Now then!"

With that, he turned back around, let go with his hands, took the bottle, and raised it to his lips. He threw his head back and lifted his free hand for balance. One of the footmen, who had bent down to pick up broken glass, froze in that position, his eyes locked on the window and on Dolokhov's back. Anatole stood rigid, eyes wide. The Englishman watched from the side, lips pursed. The man who had tried to stop it all ran to a corner and threw himself face-down on the sofa. Pierre covered his face with his hands — a faint smile lingering on his features even though his expression now showed nothing but horror and fear. Everyone was completely still. Pierre took his hands away from his eyes. Dolokhov was still sitting in the same position, only his head was thrown further back until his curly hair touched his shirt collar, and the hand holding the bottle rose higher and higher, trembling with the effort. The bottle was visibly emptying, rising higher still, his head tilting back even more. "Why is it taking so long?" thought Pierre. It felt like more than half an hour had passed. Suddenly Dolokhov's spine arched backward and his arm shook convulsively; this was enough to make his whole body start sliding on the sloped ledge. As he began to slip, his head and arm wavered even more with the strain. One hand moved as if to grab the windowsill, then pulled back without touching it. Pierre covered his eyes again and told himself he would never open them. Then suddenly he felt a commotion all around. He looked up: Dolokhov was standing on the windowsill, his face pale but radiant.
"It's empty."
He tossed the bottle to the Englishman, who caught it neatly. Dolokhov jumped back into the room. He reeked of rum.
"Bravo! Well done! Now that's a bet! Unbelievable!" came the shouts from all sides.
The Englishman pulled out his purse and began counting out the money. Dolokhov stood frowning, saying nothing. Pierre leapt up onto the windowsill.
"Who wants to bet me? I'll do the same thing!" he cried suddenly. "Forget the bet — just like that! Someone bring me a bottle! I'll do it! Bring a bottle!"
"Let him try, let him try," said Dolokhov with a smile.
"Are you insane? Absolutely not! No one's letting you do that! You get dizzy just on a staircase!" several voices cried at once.
"I'll drink it! Bring me a bottle of rum!" Pierre yelled, slamming the table with a drunken, determined fist and getting ready to climb out the window.
They grabbed him by the arms, but he was so strong that everyone who touched him went flying.
"No, you'll never manage him like that," said Anatole. "Wait — I'll talk him round. Listen! I'll take your bet tomorrow, but right now we're all going to ——'s."
"Let's go then!" cried Pierre. "Let's go! And we're bringing the bear!"
He grabbed the bear, lifted it in his arms, and began dancing around the room with it.
